extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of public opinion, journalists, policymakers, and social scientists
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles governing how information, social structures, and communication technologies shape the formation and circulation of public opinion. Focuses on constraints (time, attention, infrastructure, social sets), mechanisms (imitation, leadership), and linguistic/technical factors that distort or compress meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extreme measures required for nationwide uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: "Probably this is the largest and the most intensive effort to carry quickly a fairly uniform set of ideas to all the people of a nation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Creel's World War I machinery: Division of News issuing thousands of releases, 75,000 Four Minute Men delivering hundreds of thousands of speeches, annotated addresses delivered by Boy Scouts, fortnightly periodicals to teachers, lantern slides, posters, window cards, cartoons, seals and buttons, plus parallel efforts (Liberty Loans, Red Cross, Y.M.C.A.). Implies that achieving near-uniform public opinion in crisis requires vast, coordinated resources of money, personnel, and organizational ingenuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure and means of communication shape circulation of ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: "Travel and trade, the mails, the wires, and radio, railroads, highways, ships, motor cars, and in the coming generation aeroplanes, are, of course, of the utmost influence on the circulation of ideas."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each transport/communication medium affects both the supply and quality of information; changes in passports, customs, new railways/ports/shipping lines, cable censorship or cost, highways, and air travel alter how ideas spread. Technical, economic, and political conditions mediate these effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopoly, cost, and supply act as barriers to exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: "The monopolizing of cables... of ports, fuel stations, mountain passes, canals, straits, river courses, terminals, market places means a good deal more than the enrichment of a group of business men... It means a barrier upon the exchange of news and opinion. But monopoly is not the only barrier. Cost and available supply are even greater ones."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access to information can be blocked by control of physical/communication chokepoints and by prohibitive costs or limited capacity (even absent formal monopolies). Policy changes (tariffs, subsidies) and infrastructure control therefore have direct political and informational consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Income determines access to the world of information
rubrics_metrics.description: "The size of a man's income has considerable effect on his access to the world beyond his neighborhood. With money he can overcome almost every tangible obstacle of communication..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money allows travel, purchase of books/periodicals, and broader engagement; community income likewise affects possible communication. However, how income is spent depends on individuals' ideas and tastes, so economic capacity interacts with preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-imposed limitations (lack of curiosity) restrict information uptake
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages describing groups who "spend most of their spare time and spare money on motoring and comparing motor cars, on bridge-whist and post-mortems, on moving-pictures and potboilers... They cannot really be said to suffer from censorship... They suffer from anemia, from lack of appetite and curiosity for the human scene."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all barriers are external; habitual choices and cultural pastimes limit exposure even where access exists. Such apathy reduces the effective reach of information despite available channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: The social set determines admissible authorities and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the social set... it is finally decided in each phase of a discussion which authorities and which sources of information are admissible, and which not."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership in a social set defines whose opinions count ('people are saying') and which information sources are trusted. This gatekeeping function organizes how individuals interpret and prioritize news and opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social sets are organized around family tradition and norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions in the social set encounter the canons of 'Family Tradition, Respectability, Propriety, Dignity, Taste and Form' which the set implants in children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social standing and familial/cultural norms shape long-term dispositions toward information, what is considered respectable knowledge, and which topics are acceptable, thereby influencing public opinion formation across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social leaders act as custodians/interpreters and link sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Social leaders... are recognized as the custodians and the interpreters of [a set's] social pattern... They act as a kind of ministry of foreign affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders are sensitive to threats to the set's integrity and to other sets' practices; they translate and mediate between sets, creating channels of information and influence. Their behaviors and endorsements carry disproportionate weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radiant points of conventionality and imitation transmit standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of the sets are so placed that they become what Professor Ross has called 'radiant points of conventionality.' The social superior is likely to be imitated by the social inferior... imitation does not stop at frontiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain socially dominant groups (cosmopolitans, high society, influential elites) function as models; their opinions and practices diffuse downward and across boundaries, including internationally, shaping broader public standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited time and attention constrain exposure to public affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey evidence (college students; business/professional men) indicates that large majorities estimate about a quarter of an hour a day reading newspapers; many readers read only two or three papers daily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because individuals devote little daily time to news, depth and breadth of information uptake are limited; this shapes how much factual basis underlies public opinions and increases reliance on heuristics and social cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of newspaper space broadly corresponds to reader interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of newspapers showed allocations (after excluding advertisements) that put roughly 76.5% of edited space on items dealing with public affairs, roughly matching readers' stated interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors' space allocations tend to mirror the aggregate preferences of urban readers (war, politics, business, opinion). However, aggregate space does not guarantee individual attention; distributional and temporal constraints remain important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers are principal but not sole channels of public information
rubrics_metrics.description: The newspapers are... the principal ones. Magazines, the public forum, the chautauqua, the church, political gatherings, trade union meetings, women's clubs, and news serials in the moving picture houses supplement the press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full account of public opinion formation must include diverse supplementary channels, though newspapers typically play the leading role in everyday exposure to public affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telegraphic coding and compression telescope meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Press service news is, therefore, usually coded... A few words must often stand for a whole succession of acts, thoughts, feelings and consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To save cost and speed transmission, dispatches are shortened, coded and later expanded; this condensation loses contextual detail and nuance, forcing readers to make imaginative inferences and potentially misjudge the weight of events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation, coding and transmission processes distort substance
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance has been culled from a long speech in a foreign tongue, translated, coded, and then decoded... No matter how rich or subtle... the more his meaning will suffer as it is sluiced into standard speech and then distributed again among alien minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign speeches and complex messages lose precision through translation and syndication; operators, coders, and editors contribute to cumulative loss/distortion that can alter public interpretation, sometimes with serious diplomatic consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words are ambiguous and evoke different images across audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Words, like currency, are turned over and over again, to evoke one set of images to-day, another to-morrow... When we use the word 'Mexico' what picture does it evoke in a resident of New York?... The word 'alien' had widely varying definitions among college students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identical terms can summon very different associations depending on cultural background, education, and prejudice; legal terms may be more exact, but common political vocabulary is subject to shifting 'word-exchange' values that impede mutual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: National rhetorical styles affect interpretation ('word-currency' differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some nations constitutionally tend to understate, others to overstate. Nations that overstate suffer from inflation in their language... Expressions must be mentally revalued across languages and rhetorical habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers must mentally 'exchange' rhetorical intensities when interpreting foreign press; failure to do so can lead to exaggeration or underestimation of the significance of foreign statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lucidity—ability to dissociate superficial analogies—is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to dissociate superficial analogies, attend to differences and appreciate variety is lucidity of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound public opinion depends on the capacity to discriminate among crude perceptions and vague analogies; this skill varies widely across individuals and is central to interpreting sparse or compressed news intelligently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social position and contact bias moral judgment over constructive thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Since position and contact play so big a part in determining what can be seen, heard, read, and experienced... it is no wonder that moral judgment is so much more common than constructive thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because social networks define what information is accessible and permissible, collective moral judgments often substitute for sustained, detached analysis; achieving constructive thought requires conscious effort to 'liquidate judgments' and regain curiosity and equanimity.
